UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE​
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Processes                                           Docket No. AD26-7-000


                      COMMENTS OF WOLF MERIDIAN GROUP
                                      Justin Trout, Founder & Principal
                                               August 16, 2026

I. Introduction and Summary
     Wolf Meridian Group respectfully submits these comments in response to the Commission's July
30, 2026 notice inviting post-technical-conference comments concerning PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.
governance and stakeholder processes. Wolf Meridian Group is an independent infrastructure and
strategic analysis firm focused on power, compute, infrastructure, and the decision processes that shape
large-scale energy development.
     These comments are submitted from the perspective of an independent outside participant. Wolf
Meridian Group does not represent a PJM member, market participant, utility, governmental entity, or
other stakeholder organization in this proceeding. Its recommendations are offered in response to the
Commission's request for concrete, actionable reforms and draw on practical analysis of grid capacity,
large-load growth, load forecasting, infrastructure readiness, and the physical systems required to
support new electrical demand.
    These comments focus on the Commission's questions concerning accountability and
responsiveness in PJM governance, transparency, state participation, committee delay, and the potential
use of fast-path or time-bound stakeholder procedures. Wolf Meridian Group recommends that PJM
consider a permanent critical-issue decision track that builds on the experience of existing Critical Issue
Fast Path processes while using objective activation criteria, a defined decision schedule, a common
technical record, formal state and consumer consultation, a written Board disposition, and
post-implementation review.
    A faster process should not mean a less rigorous process. The objective should be to compress
sequencing, reduce duplicative review, and support decisions against one transparent technical record.
For matters with material reliability, market, or infrastructure consequences, delay can itself create risk.
A well-defined expedited process can preserve stakeholder input while creating a dependable path from
problem identification to decision.

II. Why Governance Speed Matters in a Large-Load Era
    The Commission convened the July 23, 2026 technical conference specifically to examine whether
PJM's governance mechanics and stakeholder processes allow the organization to address operational
and market needs in a timely and efficient manner. The conference agenda asked whether existing
committee structures contribute to delay and whether PJM should increase the use of fast-path or
time-bound review procedures for high-importance topics. Those questions are especially important as


                                 Wolf Meridian Group | Docket No. AD26-7-000 | 1
 electricity demand becomes more dynamic and as large new loads can alter planning assumptions on
timelines that do not align neatly with traditional committee cycles.
    PJM has already recognized this problem in practice. Its Critical Issue Fast Path process for Large
Load Additions was initiated to develop reliability-focused solutions for integrating large loads rapidly
and reliably. PJM has also continued to refine its load forecasting process, including updated large-load
adjustments, a Data Center Accuracy Report, and a 2026 mid-year load forecast update. These efforts
demonstrate both the scale of the challenge and the need for governance processes that can absorb new
technical information without forcing every urgent issue through a long sequence of separate
committees.
     The governance lesson is broader than any one class of load. When assumptions affecting reliability,
resource adequacy, transmission planning, market design, or customer costs change materially, PJM
needs a process capable of separating verified information from projections, rapidly developing
alternatives, obtaining state and stakeholder input, and reaching a reasoned decision on a known
schedule.

III. Recommended Reform: A Permanent Critical-Issue Decision Track
A. Objective Activation Criteria
     PJM should establish written criteria for activating an expedited decision process. The process
should be available when an issue presents a material reliability or market consequence, requires action
within a defined time horizon, crosses multiple PJM committees or functional areas, or presents a
meaningful risk that delay will increase system cost, reliability exposure, or implementation difficulty.
Stakeholders should be able to request activation, but the Board or PJM management should make the
activation decision through a short written finding.
    Objective activation criteria would improve predictability and help prevent an expedited process
from becoming either an extraordinary tool used too rarely or a routine shortcut used too often. The
standard stakeholder process should remain the default. A critical-issue track should be reserved for
matters where the need for expedited action can be demonstrated.
B. A Defined Decision Schedule
     A critical-issue track should begin with a published issue charter identifying the problem, decision
authority, scope, governing documents implicated, lead technical group, required data, and target
decision date. As a default framework, PJM could target a 90-day process unless the Board determines
that a different schedule is necessary. A model schedule could include the following milestones:
 ●​Day 0: Publish the issue charter, scope, decision authority, and schedule.
 ●​By Day 15: Publish the common technical record and identify material data gaps.
 ●​By Day 45: Publish a limited set of technically viable alternatives with reliability, market,
   implementation, and cost implications.
 ●​By Day 60: Complete a defined consultation period for states, consumer advocates, and other
   affected stakeholder groups.
 ●​By Day 75: Complete stakeholder voting or written position submissions, as applicable.
 ●​By Day 90: Publish a Board or PJM disposition and, where Commission action is required, direct
   the appropriate filing.


                                Wolf Meridian Group | Docket No. AD26-7-000 | 2
     Extensions should be permitted, but they should require a written explanation identifying the
unresolved issue and a new decision date. A deadline that can disappear without explanation is not a
meaningful deadline.
C. One Common Technical Record
     Expedited governance will only work if participants are debating policy choices from the same
technical baseline. PJM should therefore create a common technical record at the beginning of each
critical-issue process. That record should identify the assumptions, data sources, uncertainty ranges, and
known limitations that will be used to compare alternatives.
     For issues involving significant load growth, the record should distinguish between verified system
data and projected demand, and projected demand should be categorized by confidence based on
objective development milestones. The purpose is not to exclude uncertain future demand from
planning. The purpose is to prevent highly uncertain projections and near-certain obligations from being
treated as though they carry the same evidentiary weight.
     The technical record should also identify, where relevant, the effects of each option on reliability,
generation adequacy, transmission needs, implementation timing, customer cost exposure, and the
ability to revise the decision as better information becomes available. Confidential commercial
information can be protected, but the assumptions used for regional planning should be disclosed at a
level sufficient for meaningful review.
D. Formal State and Consumer Consultation Without Creating a Veto
     The Commission's agenda appropriately asks how states should participate in PJM's governance and
stakeholder processes. On critical issues, state participation should be structured rather than informal.
The expedited process should include a defined consultation window for the Organization of PJM
States, Inc., individual state commissions where appropriate, and state consumer advocates. Their
written positions should become part of the decisional record.
    This consultation should not convert regional grid governance into a state-by-state veto structure.
PJM must retain the independence required to perform its regional functions. But where a decision may
materially affect retail customers, state resource planning, infrastructure development, or local
implementation, the process should require those concerns to be surfaced early enough to influence the
analysis rather than after a preferred solution has effectively been selected.
E. A Written Board Disposition
     At the conclusion of a critical-issue process, the Board should publish a concise decisional
memorandum. The memorandum should identify the alternatives considered, the principal technical
findings, major stakeholder disagreements, material uncertainties, the reasons for the selected path, and
any matters that require Commission approval or further stakeholder work.
    This would directly improve accountability and transparency. It would also create an institutional
record that later Boards, states, stakeholders, and the Commission can use to understand why a decision
was made under a particular set of facts.
F. Mandatory Post-Implementation Review
    Fast decisions are sometimes made with incomplete information. That is acceptable when the
uncertainty is acknowledged and the decision is revisited. Each critical-issue process should therefore

                                Wolf Meridian Group | Docket No. AD26-7-000 | 3
 include a scheduled post-implementation review, ordinarily within 12 to 18 months. PJM should
compare forecast assumptions with observed results, identify unintended effects, and determine whether
the governing rule or process should be modified.
    This creates a feedback loop between planning and reality. It also reduces the pressure to make
every expedited decision permanent on day one.

IV. Large Loads Demonstrate Why the Reform Is Necessary
     Large-load growth provides a useful example of why governance structure and technical analysis
can no longer be separated. A single large project may implicate load forecasting, generation adequacy,
transmission planning, interconnection timing, distribution utility coordination, market rules, cost
responsibility, and state policy. If those questions are handled serially through separate processes, the
system can spend substantial time debating pieces of a problem that is operationally one problem.
    PJM's existing Large Load Additions Critical Issue Fast Path shows that expedited treatment can be
appropriate. The next step should be to convert that experience into a durable governance capability
rather than treating each new urgent issue as a one-off emergency. The critical-issue track should
provide a reusable structure for high-impact questions while allowing the technical content to vary by
issue.
     Load forecasting illustrates the need for this structure. Forecasts necessarily contain uncertainty, and
emerging large loads can change quickly as projects are announced, delayed, resized, financed,
connected, or cancelled. Governance should require decision-makers to see not only a single forecast
number, but the confidence and development maturity underlying material forecast adjustments. That
approach would improve the quality of decisions without requiring PJM to wait for perfect information
that will never exist.

V. Relationship to the Commission's Questions
    The recommendations above directly respond to several questions posed in the July 23 technical
conference agenda:
  ●​Panel 1, Question 3 - Accountability and responsiveness: objective activation criteria, a fixed
    schedule, and a written Board disposition create an auditable decision process.
  ●​Panel 2, Question 2 - Transparency: a common technical record makes assumptions, uncertainties,
    and alternative impacts visible before decisions are made.
  ●​Panel 2, Question 3 - State participation: a defined consultation window gives states and consumer
    advocates a meaningful role without compromising PJM's regional independence.
  ●​Panel 2, Questions 5 and 7 - Stakeholder-process reform and committee delay: a single issue charter
    and lead process reduce serial referrals and duplicative committee work.
  ●​Panel 2, Question 8 - Fast-path procedures: a permanent, criteria-based critical-issue track would
    institutionalize time-bound review while preserving technical rigor and stakeholder input.




                                 Wolf Meridian Group | Docket No. AD26-7-000 | 4
 VI. Conclusion
     PJM does not need to choose between inclusive governance and timely decisions. It needs a process
designed to do both. The Commission should encourage PJM to consider formalizing a permanent
critical-issue decision track that includes objective activation criteria, a published schedule, one
common technical record, structured state and consumer consultation, a written Board disposition, and a
mandatory post-implementation review.
    The physical system is changing rapidly, and governance processes must be capable of responding
to new information without sacrificing transparency or accountability. Large loads, changing forecasts,
new generation needs, transmission constraints, and emerging infrastructure demands will continue to
create difficult regional decisions. A durable fast-path structure can help PJM address those decisions
more efficiently while preserving meaningful stakeholder participation and a clear public record.


Respectfully submitted,
/s/ Justin Trout
